a_records.quote: Counterexample 3.1. Consider the baseline distribution function as Fb (x) = 1 − exp(1 − xa ), x ≥ 1, a > 0. For this, when 0 < a ≤ 1, the hazard rate function is decreasing. Let {X1 , X2 , X3 } and {Y1 , Y2 , Y3 } be the collections of dependent random variables with Xi ∼ Fbα ((x−λi )/θ) and Yi ∼ Fbα ((x−µi )/θ), for i = 1, 2, 3 with generators ψ1 (x) = e(1/a1 )(1−ex ) and ψ2 (x) = e(1/a2 )(1−ex ), respectively, where x > 0, 0 < a1 , a2 ≤ 1. Here, ψ1 and ψ2 both are log-concave. Assume a1 = 0.001 and a2 = 0.5. Then, φ2 ◦ ψ1 (x) is sub-additive, and hence is not super-additive. Set λ = (3, 4, 5), µ = (6, 7, 8), θ = 6, α = 8 and a = 0.9. Thus, all the conditions of Theorem 3.17 are satisfied except super-additivity of φ2 ◦ ψ1 (x) and the restriction on α. Now, we plote the graphs of F̄X2:3 (x) and F̄Y2:3 (x) in Figure 2a. The graphs cross each other, which implies that Theorem 3.17 does not hold.
a_records.family: ELS marginals; generators ψi(x) = e^{(1/ai)(1−e^x)}, 0 < ai <= 1; lower-truncated Weibull baseline Fb(x) = 1 − exp(1 − x^a), x >= 1

b_records.ambiguity: With λ = (3,4,5), µ = (6,7,8), the hypothesis µ ≼w λ of Theorem 3.17 appears also to fail under the printed Definition 2.2 (µ has the larger upper-tail sums), so the example may violate the majorization hypothesis as well as the two conditions the authors list.
